setting.name: Bellweather
setting.summary: A small village of a square, a manor, an inn, a greenhouse, a church vestry and a doctor's surgery. Edmund Vale of Vale Manor is dead; the investigation begins the next morning.

rules.text: Arsenic taken in drink brings on illness some hours later, not at once.

people.name: Clara Vale
people.voice: Composed and guarded; courteous but says little, quietly deflecting private matters. Speaks briefly.
people.public: Edmund’s younger sister. She manages the manor and has asked that its private affairs remain private.

people.name: Rowan Pike
people.voice: A plain-spoken working man; blunt and practical, short sentences, no flourishes.
people.public: The manor’s groundskeeper. His bandaged hand and green coat have become subjects of village conversation.

people.name: Silas Voss
people.voice: A precise, careful solicitor; measured and a touch formal, but concise — never rambling.
people.public: A precise, courteous solicitor who keeps an office in the vestry. He handled Edmund’s estate accounts.

people.name: Ada Finch
people.voice: A warm, chatty innkeeper; colloquial and quick to share impressions, though she runs on a little.
people.public: The Rook & Lantern’s proprietor. She knows everyone’s habits and is certain she saw something useful last night.

people.name: Dr Iris Marsh
people.voice: Measured and clinical; direct and concise, stays to what she observed.
people.public: Methodical and direct. She examined Edmund’s body and treated a patient at the greenhouse last night.

people.name: Arthur Bell
people.voice: A plain, gruff country constable; terse and matter-of-fact, everyday speech — never bureaucratic or long-winded.
people.public: Bell has secured the manor and asked you to investigate. He will hear an accusation when you can explain it with evidence.

people.name: Edmund Vale
people.public: Master of Vale Manor, found dead the morning the investigation begins.

objects.name: Study brandy decanter
objects.desc: Cut-glass decanter on Edmund's study desk, from which he poured his nightcap.

objects.name: Estate account ledger
objects.desc: The Vale estate's accounts, kept by Silas Voss.

objects.name: Tin of arsenical weedkiller
objects.desc: A tin kept on the greenhouse shelf for the gravel paths.

objects.name: Letter for Miss Vale
objects.desc: A private letter held for Clara at the inn.

objects.name: Taproom tab slate
objects.desc: A chalk slate behind the Rook's bar where Ada notes each evening's tabs.

objects.name: Vestry office day-book
objects.desc: Silas Voss's bound record of his office hours and work, kept on his vestry desk.

objects.name: Stoppered glass phial
objects.desc: A small blackened phial raked from the ashes of the vestry stove.

objects.name: Edmund's audit notes
objects.desc: Pencilled sheets in Edmund's hand comparing the ledger with the bank book.

objects.name: Charred envelope
objects.desc: The burnt remains of an envelope in the manor's morning-room grate.

objects.name: Cellar hatch key
objects.desc: Iron key to the padlock on the Rook's cellar hatch, kept by Ada.

objects.name: Spare kitchen slate
objects.desc: A smaller chalk slate Ada normally keeps in the Rook's kitchen for orders.

objects.name: Constable's notebook page
objects.desc: A page torn from Constable Bell's pocket-book, asking Dr Marsh to assist the inquiry.

attitudes.content: He has been quietly drawing on estate funds for two years.
The estate accounts do not balance and Voss must explain them.
Edmund's audit will expose his theft and ruin him.
Poison Edmund's brandy before the audit can proceed.
Be seen working late at his vestry office as usual.
Host supper for his sister and his solicitor.
Take his usual brandy before bed.
Collect her private letter from the inn without her brother knowing.
Return home and retire for the night.
Wake her brother for breakfast.
Finish the potting before he leaves the estate's service.
Attend to her patients as called.
Keep the taproom running through the evening.
An evening pint at the Rook after his rounds.
Secure the scene of a suspicious death.
Ashamed that he sat over pints at the Rook when he should have been walking his rounds.
Keep her visit to the inn and her letter unknown to the village.
Say nothing of Miss Vale's visit, as she promised.
Write up his day-book so it shows him at his vestry desk through the whole evening.
Keep out of the manor's affairs now that Mr Vale has dismissed him.
Burn the phial in his vestry stove so nothing of it remains.
Keep her brother's private estate papers out of the constable's hands and away from village gossip.
Leave Bellweather to train as a nurse in London, though Edmund forbade it.
Burn the London envelope so no one in the village learns she means to leave.
Pike's cut is bleeding badly and she must go to him at once.
Put the tab slate out of sight before anyone asks who came in last night, to keep her promise to Miss Vale.
Lock the cellar hatch and keep the key, so nobody finds the slate.
Put off any search that would have him account for his own evening, until it is already known.
Hand family papers only to someone who has already shown discretion about her own secret.
Keep her surgery wall clock ten minutes fast, so that she is never late to a patient.
Hang a freshly chalked spare slate on the bar nail so the missing tab slate draws no questions.
Keep it to herself that the surgery clock runs fast, so patients who read it hurry as she does.
Tell anyone who asks that last night was quiet and Miss Vale never came in, and point them to the slate on the nail.
Keep her patients' affairs confidential and talk to no stranger about her night calls without the constable's authority.
Give the investigator his written say-so for the doctor, since it asks nothing about his own evening.

events.summary: Edmund hosts supper for Clara and Silas at the manor.
Edmund keeps Silas in the study to question the estate accounts.
While Edmund steps out, Silas tips weedkiller into the study brandy decanter.
Silas works late at his vestry office.
Clara collects a private letter from Ada and sits by the inn fire.
Clara returns to the manor and goes to bed.
Edmund pours and drinks his brandy nightcap in the study.
Edmund succumbs to arsenic poisoning in his bed.
Rowan pots seedlings in the greenhouse and cuts his hand on a pane.
Iris sees evening patients at her surgery.
Iris stitches Rowan's cut hand at the greenhouse.
Iris returns to her surgery and writes up notes.
Ada tends the taproom bar all evening.
Bell drinks his pint at the Rook's bar.
Clara finds Edmund dead in his bed.
Iris examines the body and suspects poison.
Bell secures the manor.
Ada chalks the evening's tabs on the slate behind the bar.
Before leaving, Clara asks Ada to tell no one she came in tonight.
At his vestry desk, Silas writes day-book entries timed from 21:00, as though he had worked there all evening.
Before supper, Silas fills a small glass phial from the weedkiller tin on the empty greenhouse's shelf.
Silas pushes the empty phial, wrapped in paper, into the vestry stove's fire.
After finding Edmund, Clara takes the pencilled sheets from his study desk and locks them in her bureau.
After Bell leaves, Clara burns the London envelope in the morning-room grate and keeps the letter hidden in her sleeve.
Hurrying out, Iris wedges a timed card in her surgery door and leaves her watch on the desk.
Hearing of the death, Ada takes the unwiped tab slate off its nail and stands it face to the wall in the cellar.
Heavy rain after midnight soaks the surgery doorway while Dr Marsh sleeps inside.
At five in the morning Ada takes two hogsheads down the yard chute and leaves its flap unbolted.
Coming up from the cellar, Ada padlocks the hatch and pockets the key.
Back at the surgery, Iris logs Pike's call in her case-book, reading the call time off her fast wall clock.
Ada chalks a few nameless tabs on her smaller kitchen slate and hangs it on the bar nail.
Asked the time at her surgery, Iris waits for St Alden's quarter-chime and gives it without mentioning her clock.
Asked about last night, Ada says it was quiet, denies Miss Vale came in, and points at the bar slate.
At twenty to nine in the morning, Iris speaks through the half-open surgery door and refuses questions without the constable's authority.
In the square, Bell pencils a line to Dr Marsh in his pocket-book and tears out the page.

signs.title: The doctor’s examination notes
signs.text: Examination of the deceased, Edmund Vale, reveals no external wounds or signs of violence. Internal congestion and irritation of the stomach lining are consistent with a poison taken by mouth. I estimate he died around one o'clock, though the poison itself was taken some hours earlier, between ten past nine and twenty past nine.

reactions.silas: A grim business, Doctor's notes or not. I was at my vestry desk by nine, as my day-book will show — you may check it against the sexton's own comings and goings if you doubt me. I can hardly account for what happened at the manor after I left.

signs.show: The doctor's notes say Edmund Vale had no wounds, but stomach irritation consistent with poison taken by mouth some hours before he died, between ten past and twenty past nine. Does that time mean anything to you?

signs.speaker: iris
signs.title: Dr Marsh on the body
signs.text: Mr Vale died around one o'clock, but whatever he swallowed was taken well before that, between ten past nine and twenty past nine — there's not a mark on him, only the signs of a poison taken by mouth.
signs.ask: Doctor, what did you find when you examined Edmund?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says Mr Vale died from poison taken by mouth, sometime between ten past and twenty past nine last night. Does that match what you know?
signs.confront: You told me Mr Vale died from poison taken by mouth, between ten past and twenty past nine last night. Is that the whole of what you can tell me?

signs.speaker: bell
signs.title: Arthur Bell on the evening
signs.text: I was about the village on my rounds, same as any night, and I stopped in at the Rook for a pint before I finished up. Nothing out of the ordinary that I noticed.
signs.confront: You told me you were on your rounds and stopped at the Rook for a pint, with nothing out of the ordinary. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Constable Bell says he did his rounds as usual and stopped at the Rook for a pint, noticing nothing unusual that night. Does that match what you saw?

signs.speaker: iris
signs.title: Dr Iris Marsh on the evening
signs.text: I was called out to a cut hand that wanted stitching, and after that I was back at my surgery seeing to my notes and whatever patients came to the door. I can't say more than that without going into who came and why, and I won't do that without the constable's say-so.
signs.confront: You told me you tended a cut hand, then were at your surgery with notes and patients, but wouldn't say more. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says she was called out to stitch a cut hand, then returned to her surgery for notes and patients, but won't say more without the constable's leave. Do you know anything about that evening?

signs.speaker: ada
signs.title: Ada Finch on the evening
signs.text: Oh, quiet as anything it was - just my regulars in for a pint, nothing to speak of. Miss Vale? No, didn't see her at all, you can check the slate on the nail there.
signs.confront: You told me it was a quiet night with just your regulars, and that you never saw Miss Vale. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Mrs Finch says it was a quiet night at the Rook with just her regulars, and that she never saw Miss Vale at all. Does that tally with what you know?

signs.speaker: silas
signs.title: Silas Voss on the evening
signs.text: I was at the vestry office the whole evening, catching up on the day-books after supper at the manor. You may check my entries if you wish.
signs.confront: You told me you were at the vestry office all evening working on the day-books. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Mr Voss says he spent the whole evening at the vestry office catching up on the day-books after supper at the manor. Do you know if that's true?

signs.speaker: rowan
signs.title: Rowan Pike on the evening
signs.text: Was in the greenhouse, potting seedlings. Cut my hand on a pane, got it seen to, then went home.
signs.confront: You told me you were in the greenhouse potting seedlings, cut your hand, had it tended, then went home. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Mr Pike says he was potting seedlings in the greenhouse, cut his hand on a pane, had it seen to, then went home. Does that match what you know?

signs.speaker: clara
signs.title: Clara Vale on the evening
signs.text: I supped at the manor with my brother and Mr Voss, then walked a little and turned in early. I've nothing more to tell you, I'm afraid.
signs.confront: You told me you supped at the manor, walked a little, and turned in early. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Miss Vale says she supped at the manor with her brother and Mr Voss, then walked a little before turning in early. Do you know if that's so?

signs.title: Dr Marsh on the greenhouse
signs.text: "I was fetched to the greenhouse after my evening patients. I left in such a hurry that my watch stayed on the desk. I went straight there and stitched Mr Pike's hand, a deep cut from a broken pane, for about an hour. He sat on the stool throughout. I'd have noticed if he'd moved. I was home a little after ten."
signs.speaker: iris
signs.reading: The card fixes her departure at 20:40, and the walk from the surgery to the greenhouse takes about twelve minutes, so her hour at the stool ran from about nine until ten.
signs.ask: Dr Marsh, what happened in the greenhouse that night?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says she was fetched to the greenhouse and spent about an hour stitching Mr Pike's hand there, with him seated the whole time, arriving home a little after ten. Does that match what you saw?
signs.confront: You told me you went straight to the greenhouse, left your watch behind, and stitched Mr Pike's hand there for about an hour while he sat still. Is that the whole of it?

concede.s_door_card: Very well - the card shows half past ten, not a little after, so I'll set it down plainly: I was with Mr Pike at the greenhouse from nine until ten. I said 'a little after' only because I hadn't looked closely at my own note, not to hide anything.

reactions.rowan: Aye, that's right. I sat still the whole time, hand throbbing something awful. Doctor'll tell you the same - I never moved off that stool.

signs.title: Mrs Finch on Miss Vale
signs.text: "Miss Vale come in just after nine — five past, I'd say — for a letter I keep by for her, and she sat by the fire with it till the church struck ten. Never said a word, bless her, just read it over and over."
signs.speaker: ada
signs.unlock: Once you point out Miss Vale's entry on her own slate, Mrs Finch sees the visit is known anyway and stops keeping her promise.
signs.ask: Mrs Finch, what can you tell me about Miss Vale?
signs.show: Mrs Finch says Miss Vale came in just after nine for a letter she keeps by for her, and sat reading it by the fire until the church struck ten without saying a word. Do you know anything about that?
signs.confront: You told me you were at the manor all evening, but Mrs Finch says you came in just after nine for a letter and sat reading it by the fire until ten. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.clara: Yes. I went for a letter of my own, and I'd rather it stayed my own affair. It has nothing to do with my brother.
reactions.silas: Miss Vale's evening is her own business, not mine. I was at my desk in the vestry the whole time, as my day-book shows.

signs.title: Constable Bell on the taproom
signs.text: "Had my pint at the Rook. Half eight till ten past ten. Mrs Finch behind the bar the whole time. Never left it."
signs.speaker: bell
signs.unlock: Shown his own tab chalked on the slate, Bell stops dodging the question and grudgingly admits where he spent the evening.
signs.ask: Constable Bell, what happened in the taproom that night?
signs.show: Constable Bell says he had his pint at the Rook from half eight until ten past ten, with Mrs Finch behind the bar the whole time and never leaving it. Does that match what you saw?
signs.confront: You told me it was quiet with just your regulars, but Constable Bell says he was there from half eight to ten past ten and you never left the bar. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.ada: That's right, love, never left the bar all night. Steady as you like, weren't it, Constable - nothing out of the ordinary happened here.

signs.title: The tab slate in the cellar
signs.text: Behind the barrels in the Rook's cellar, a chalk slate stands face to the wall. It has not been wiped. Among the entries: 'Const. B. — 2 pts — pd 10.10' and 'Miss V. — cocoa 9.05 — letter handed over'.
signs.unlock: You lift the unbolted flap and slide down the barrel chute into the cellar, where you search behind the barrels and find the slate.
signs.show: I found a chalk slate hidden behind the barrels in your cellar, unwiped, showing 'Const. B. paid 10.10' and 'Miss V., cocoa 9.05, letter handed over.' Can you explain why this was hidden away rather than kept on its nail?

reactions.ada: Oh — that's the cellar slate, that. I'll own it, I put it down there and said Miss Vale never came in, but she asked me to keep quiet about her visit, and I don't break a promise to a lady, not even for you. Cocoa and a letter, that's all it was — nothing wicked in that.

signs.title: The vestry day-book
signs.text: Open on Mr Voss's vestry desk, in his neat hand: '9.00 p.m. — at desk. Harcourt conveyance drafted, 9.05 to 9.40. Michaelmas rents entered, 9.40 to 10.30.' The ink on the whole page is the same shade, and there is no blot anywhere on it.
signs.show: This is Mr Voss's day-book, open to last night, with times for the Harcourt conveyance and the Michaelmas rents written in one steady hand with no blots. Does that match what you know of his evening?

reactions.silas: That is precisely how I keep my day-book, entered as I go, without blot or delay. I worked at that desk through the whole evening on estate business, as the entries plainly show. I've nothing further to add.

signs.title: Mr Pike on the study window
signs.text: "Vestry? No. I sat on that stool facing the lawn while the doctor stitched me. Study lamp was lit. The solicitor was in that window from a bit after nine till half past. Mr Vale came and went. Didn't want to say. Not my house any more."
signs.speaker: rowan
signs.unlock: Pike has been keeping out of manor business since his dismissal, but once you tell him the solicitor's book puts him at the vestry all evening, he says bluntly what he saw.
signs.reading: Dr Marsh confirms Pike sat on the greenhouse stool the whole hour from nine, and the greenhouse stands three minutes from the manor, facing the study, so he was placed to see its window.
signs.ask: Mr Pike, what did you notice about the study window?
signs.confront: You told me you sat facing the lawn while the doctor stitched you and saw the solicitor in that window from after nine till half past. Is that everything you saw?

concede.s_iris_rowan: Right, since the doctor's own account bears it out - Vale was at his window from five past nine to half past nine. I didn't want to name him outright, seeing as it's his house now and not mine to be talking about his comings and goings.

signs.show: Mr Pike says he sat facing the lawn while the doctor stitched him, with the study lamp lit, and saw the solicitor in that window from after nine till half past. Does that match what you know?

reactions.silas: Mr Pike is mistaken, or the light played tricks on him. My day-book shows plainly where I was that evening, and I stand by it.

signs.title: Edmund's pencilled sheets
signs.text: Three sheets in Edmund's hand. There are two columns, 'Ledger (Voss)' and 'Bank book', and against each quarter's rents the figures differ. The sheets total the gap at £1,140 over two years. At the foot: 'Put to V. tonight after supper. Books to Harcourt & Lowe Monday if not answered.'
signs.unlock: Miss Vale locked her brother's papers away to keep the family's affairs private. You have kept her London letter to yourself, and you tell her that Mr Pike saw the solicitor in the study although his day-book puts him at the vestry. She then unlocks her bureau and hands you the sheets.

reactions.clara: Yes — I took those from his desk after I found him. They were his private business with Mr Voss, and I saw no reason the whole village should paw through our affairs before you'd even asked.
reactions.silas: Edmund's arithmetic, not mine. I have managed those ledgers scrupulously for years, and I resent the implication otherwise. If discrepancies exist, they are clerical, and I should have welcomed the chance to reconcile them with him myself, in good time.

signs.show: These pencilled sheets in Edmund's hand set his ledger against the bank book and total a gap of £1,140 over two years, with a note to put it to 'V.' after supper that night. Do you know what this concerns?

signs.title: Glass in the vestry stove
signs.text: Under the cold ash in the vestry stove, with charred paper around it, lies a small stoppered glass phial, blackened but unbroken. A dry grey-white crust clings inside it, and when unstoppered it gives off a faint smell of garlic.
signs.unlock: Bell stalled at every search that might have him explain his evening. Once he has owned up to his pints at the Rook and heard that Pike's account contradicts the day-book, he agrees to search Mr Voss's office and rakes out the stove with you.
signs.show: Buried under cold ash in the vestry stove, I found a small unbroken glass phial with charred paper around it, holding a dry crust that smells faintly of garlic. Can you tell me what this phial contained?

reactions.silas: Weedkiller is kept in every glasshouse in the parish, Inspector; I could not tell you how that came to be in my stove. I burn a great deal of waste paper there, as any man with a fire does.

signs.title: Miss Vale at the grate
signs.text: When you come into the morning room, Miss Vale is kneeling at the grate. She stands up quickly. An envelope is curling black in the flames, and a folded paper disappears into her sleeve. "Nothing of Edmund's," she says, and she will say no more.
signs.show: Miss Vale was seen kneeling at the grate, burning an envelope and slipping a folded paper into her sleeve, saying only that it was nothing of Edmund's. Do you know what that was about?
signs.confront: I saw you kneeling at the grate burning an envelope and slipping a paper into your sleeve, saying it was nothing of Edmund's. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.clara: It was a private letter of mine, nothing of Edmund's affairs. I'd rather not say more than that.

signs.title: The letter from London
signs.text: Typed on hospital notepaper: 'Nightingale Training School, St Thomas's Hospital. Madam, we are pleased to accept you as a probationer nurse from the first of October. Kindly confirm by return.' It is addressed to Miss C. Vale, care of the Rook & Lantern, Bellweather.
signs.unlock: Once she hears that Mrs Finch has spoken of the letter held at the inn, Miss Vale would rather show it to you than have the village guess at it. She takes it from her sleeve.
signs.show: This is a typed letter from St Thomas's Nightingale Training School accepting Miss Vale as a probationer nurse from October, addressed to her care of the Rook & Lantern. Can you tell me what this letter meant to you?

reactions.ada: That's Miss Vale's letter, right enough — I kept it for her like she asked, and she came in quiet for it and sat by the fire a while. I didn't read it, mind, only held it safe till she called.
reactions.clara: Yes, that letter is mine. I collected it at the Rook, quietly, because Edmund had forbidden me to go — I'd rather that stayed between us if it can.

signs.title: Card in the surgery door
signs.text: A visiting card is still wedged in the frame of the surgery's front door. The night's rain has cockled and stained it. The pencil has run: 'Called to the greenhouse, 8.4– p.m. Back by half past ten. I.M.' The last figure of the time is a grey blur. A gold pocket watch lies open on the desk inside.
signs.reading: The rain has blurred the last figure of the time. Once the case-book's 8.50 is corrected for the fast surgery clock, it records the call at 8.40, which fills the gap.

reactions.iris: I wrote that card myself before I went out to Pike — the rain has spoiled the last figure, but I was back within the hour, as my case-book will show. I left the watch behind by mistake, nothing more.

signs.show: There's a visiting card wedged in the surgery door, rain-stained, noting a call to the greenhouse and a return by half past ten, though the last figure's smeared. Do you know anything about that?

signs.title: Behind the slate on the nail
signs.text: When you lift the slate off its nail, the wall behind it shows a clean oblong. The plaster there is less smoke-browned than the rest, and the oblong is a good two inches wider and taller than the slate in your hands. There is chalk dust on the shelf below, and white fingermarks are smudged on the ring of the cellar hatch.
signs.unlock: You take the slate down from its nail to look at it closely, and so you see the wall that was behind it.
signs.show: Behind where the slate hangs, the wall shows a clean patch larger than the slate itself, with chalk dust on the shelf and white fingermarks on the cellar hatch ring. Can you explain how that patch came to be there?

reactions.ada: That's only the little slate I chalked fresh for the nail, plain and small, I'll grant you — the proper one's a good deal bigger, kept down cellar out of the way. I've no more to say on it than that.

signs.title: Dr Marsh's case-book
signs.text: Dr Marsh's case-book lies on her surgery desk. The last entry is in her clinical hand: 'R. Pike, greenhouse. Called 8.50 p.m. (by surg. clock). Deep laceration, left palm, broken glass. Seven sutures. Dressed, and advised rest.' The entries above it cover the evening's earlier patients.
signs.reading: The church bell shows that the surgery clock runs ten minutes fast. So the call she logged at 8.50 by that clock really came at 8.40.
signs.show: Your case-book records that you were called to Mr Pike's greenhouse at ten to nine by your surgery clock, gave seven sutures for a deep laceration, and advised rest. Can you confirm this was the exact time you were called?

reactions.iris: That entry is accurate to my clock, which I keep a little fast so I'm never late to a patient. Pike's wound was as I've described — seven sutures, dressed, and sent to rest.

signs.title: The barrel-chute flap
signs.text: In the Rook's yard, the wooden flap over the cellar barrel chute hangs unbolted. The mud beside it holds fresh cart-wheel ruts. On the flap is a brewer's chalk mark: '2 hhd. 5 a.m.'
signs.unlock: The fingermarks lead to the cellar hatch, but it is padlocked, and Mrs Finch says the key has gone missing. So you go round to the yard and look for another way into the cellar.
signs.show: In the Rook's yard, the cellar barrel-chute flap is unbolted, with fresh cart-wheel ruts in the mud beside it and a brewer's chalk mark noting two hogsheads at five in the morning. Do you know who left that flap open?

reactions.ada: That's the drayman's mark, love, two hogsheads down at five, same as any brewing day — nothing more sinister than beer in that.

signs.title: The surgery wall clock
signs.text: Above Dr Marsh's desk hangs a plain wall clock with a loud tick. Its hands stand at twenty-five past nine. There is a small brass winding key on a hook beside it, and the glass has been wiped clean.
signs.reading: Dr Marsh gave the time as a quarter past nine by the church chime, while the clock's hands stood at twenty-five past. So the clock runs ten minutes fast.
signs.show: The wall clock above your desk stands at twenty-five past nine, its glass freshly wiped, with a winding key hanging beside it. Can you tell me if this clock has been recently altered?

reactions.iris: Yes, it runs some minutes fast — I keep it so deliberately, that I'm never late to a call. I didn't think it worth mentioning before now.

signs.title: The slate behind the bar
signs.text: A chalk slate hangs from a nail behind the Rook's bar. It holds only a few lines, fresh and even: 'Farmers' table: 6 pts. Darts club: 4 pts. All pd.' There are no names on it, and nothing has been wiped or crossed out.
signs.unlock: Mrs Finch nods at the slate behind the bar to back up her story, so you go round and look at it.
signs.show: This slate behind your bar shows only fresh, even lines for the farmers' table and darts club, all marked paid, with nothing crossed out or wiped. Can you tell me why this slate looks untouched compared to the other one?

reactions.ada: That's just the spare I hung up fresh, nice and tidy, so folk needn't fret over names and tabs from the night before. Nothing wiped or crossed out because there was nothing much to wipe.

signs.title: Dr Marsh tells the time
signs.text: You ask Dr Marsh the time. She glances up at the wall clock, then waits, head tilted, as St Alden's bell begins its quarter-chime. "A quarter past nine," she says, and goes back to her notes without another word.
signs.unlock: Dr Marsh reads the constable's note, unbolts the door and shows you into her consulting room. While you are there, you ask her the time.
signs.show: Dr Marsh was asked the time and glanced at the wall clock, then waited for St Alden's bell to chime the quarter before answering a quarter past nine. Do you know why she did that?
signs.confront: I asked you the time and you looked at the clock, then waited for the church bell to chime before saying a quarter past nine. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.iris: I gave you the church bell's time, not the clock's — the clock runs fast by design, and I've no cause to correct a patient's hurry over it. That is all there is to it.

signs.title: Mrs Finch on a quiet night
signs.text: "Quiet as the grave, love. Farmers' table and the darts lot, same as ever. It's all on the slate there if you don't believe me. Miss Vale? Never set foot in here. She'd have been up at the manor with her brother all evening, I should think."
signs.speaker: ada
signs.ask: Mrs Finch, how would you describe that night?
signs.confront: You told me it was a quiet night with just the farmers' table and the darts lot, and that Miss Vale was up at the manor with her brother all evening. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.clara: Mrs Finch is mistaken, or kind enough to shield me. I did go into the village that evening, though I'd rather not say why.

signs.show: Mrs Finch says the inn was quiet that night, just the farmers' table and the darts lot, and reckons Miss Vale was up at the manor with her brother all evening. Does that match what you remember?

signs.title: The surgery door
signs.text: Dr Marsh opens the surgery door a hand's width and keeps it there. "My patients' business is their own," she says. "If the constable wants me to answer questions, he can say so in writing." Then she shuts the door and bolts it.
signs.show: Dr Marsh opened her door only a hand's width and said her patients' business was their own, that the constable must ask in writing, then shut and bolted the door. Do you know why she was so guarded?
signs.confront: You opened your door only a crack and told me your patients' business was their own, that I must ask in writing, then bolted the door. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.iris: I stand by that. My patients trust me to keep their business close, and I'll not open that door wider without the constable's word in writing.

signs.title: A page from Bell's pocket-book
signs.text: A lined page torn from a constable's pocket-book. It is written in heavy pencil: 'Dr Marsh. Bearer is assisting me re Mr Vale. Oblige them. A. Bell, Const.' It has a thumbprint in pencil-lead at one corner.
signs.unlock: You tell Bell that the doctor won't talk without his written word. The request asks nothing about his own evening, so he pencils the note in the square and hands it over.
signs.show: This torn page from Constable Bell's pocket-book asks Dr Marsh to oblige the bearer in helping with Mr Vale's matter, and bears a pencil-lead thumbprint in the corner. Can you tell me how you came to have this note?

reactions.bell: Aye, that's mine right enough — my own hand and my thumb's mark an' all. Wrote it out in the square so the doctor'd know who sent the bearer, plain and simple. Nowt strange in it, just me doing my duty by Mr Vale.

signs.title: Edmund's earlier note to Voss
signs.text: Tucked beneath the pencilled sheets, a torn note in Edmund's hand: 'Voss - the rents you entered do not match what the bank shows paid in. Two years of gaps, all in your column, not the tenants'. I mean to have it out with you tonight.'
signs.unlock: once you have edmund's pencilled sheets, you know what to ask
signs.show: I've found a torn note from Edmund to Voss, accusing him of years of gaps in the rent entries and saying he meant to have it out with him that very night. Do you know anything about this dispute?

title: A Supper at Vale Manor
synopsis: Edmund Vale died in the night, after supper at Vale Manor.

clara: I live at the manor, where I keep my own bureau in the morning room for my personal papers, which I keep locked.
I found my brother dead in his bed this morning and raised the alarm, which is how the village came to know of it.
I hold the keys to my own bureau and to some of the manor's private rooms, as is proper for the lady of the house.
rowan: I'm the groundskeeper at Vale Manor and I look after the gardens and the greenhouse.
I live at the greenhouse, where I keep my tools and gardening supplies.
I keep the greenhouse key myself since I'm the one who tends it daily.
My hand's been bandaged of late, which folk have noticed and remarked on.
silas: I live and work at the vestry, where I keep my ledgers and day-book on my desk.
I keep my own vestry office key, since I'm often there working late into the evening on estate business.
bell: I'm the village constable and I keep my rounds through the square, manor, inn and other places as needed.
I live near the square, where I keep my pocket-book and notes on village matters.
I know everyone in the village in my official capacity, including Clara, Silas, Ada, Rowan and Iris.
I carry my pocket-book with me on my rounds to note anything of importance.

moods.clara: Pale and jumpy over her coffee; desperate to slip away and quietly retrieve something before anyone stirs.
moods.rowan: Sullen and eager to be gone; keeping his head down and his hands busy in the dirt.
moods.silas: Composed and businesslike, going through his morning papers as usual.
moods.iris: Brisk and tight-lipped, hurrying between patients and deflecting questions about her night calls.
moods.bell: Gruff and evasive, keen to look busy securing the scene rather than talk about his own evening.
